storage.name: storage-invitation
storage.note: A kind-1463 group invitation that lists one group storage node: `"storage": ["https://grove.example.net"]` inside the encrypted body, after `secret` (body order v, room, secret, storage), and never as a tag. A reader returns `storage` and `storageAt`, the `created_at` of the copy whose list stood. `randomHex`: the body nonce, the aux-rand. `oldReader` is what a 0.13.0 reader makes of this event: the same admission without `storage`, so an old client joins as before (today's Android does too).

storage.name: storage-full-order
storage.note: Every optional body key at once, with three nodes: body order v, room, secret, ends, destruct, relays, storage. The nodes keep the order the authority wrote them, which is the order of preference. The `expiration` tag follows `ends` as before. `randomHex`: the body nonce, the aux-rand.

storage.name: storage-withdrawn
storage.note: An empty list, `"storage": []`: the room's authority withdrew every node. It is valid, it is a list, and it stands against an older copy that named nodes (see `storage-merge`). The admission carries `storage: []` and `storageAt`. `randomHex`: the body nonce, the aux-rand.

storage.name: storage-absent
storage.note: No `storage` key: the event is byte for byte what 0.13.0 wrote. `recorded0130` holds two events recorded from 0.13.0's own encoder (`plain`, and `full` with `ends`, `destruct` and `relays`) under the fixed keys above, with the random draws in `randomHex`; today's encoder must rebuild both exactly. The generator checks that the encoder in this tree, given the same draws, writes the same two events. The admission has no `storage` and no `storageAt`, so a body without the key says nothing about nodes. `randomHex`: the body nonce, the aux-rand.

storage.name: storage-accepts
storage.note: Entries the grammar accepts, each with the `server` it implies (its host, exactly as written), alone in a hand-built envelope (`bodyJson`, then `randomHex`: the body nonce, the aux-rand). Each is canonical as it stands: `base` equals `entry`. A reader admits every one of them with `storage` set to the one entry.

storage.name: storage-entry-refusals
storage.note: One entry per case, each not canonical, alone in a hand-built envelope signed by the inviter (`bodyJson`, then `randomHex`: the body nonce, the aux-rand). A reader refuses each whole envelope (null); the encoder throws the message in `encoder`. A 0.13.0 reader, which never looks at the key, still admits each one (`oldReader`). The grammar, not what a URL parser prints, decides: `127.1`, `0x7f.0.0.1` and `127.000.0.1` are refused even though a parser would read them as 127.0.0.1.

storage.name: storage-list-refusals
storage.note: Lists the invitation may not carry, each in a hand-built envelope (`bodyJson`, then `randomHex`: the body nonce, the aux-rand): not an array, `null`, a number, an object, a number in the list, an object entry, nine entries, two entries on one host (two ports are two entries on one host, and grants are per host), and the same entry twice. A reader refuses each whole envelope; the encoder throws the message in `encoder`. A 0.13.0 reader still admits each (`oldReader`). Exactly eight entries are valid: see `eight`.

encoder.not an array: storage nodes must be a list
encoder.null: storage nodes must be a list
encoder.a number: storage nodes must be a list
encoder.an object: storage nodes must be a list
encoder.a number in the list: storage nodes must be canonical node URLs (https, or http only on this machine): 7
encoder.an object entry: storage nodes must be canonical node URLs (https, or http only on this machine): [object Object]
encoder.nine entries: a room can list at most 8 storage nodes
encoder.two ports on one host: storage nodes must not share a host name: example.net
encoder.the same entry twice: storage nodes must not share a host name: example.net

storage.name: storage-merge
storage.note: Signed copies of one invitation, heard in every order. `older` (NOW) lists A, `newer` (NOW + 10) lists B, `silent` (NOW + 20) has no `storage` key, `empty` (NOW + 30) lists `[]`, `older-empty` (NOW - 30) lists `[]` before any of them, and `tie-a` and `tie-b` (both NOW + 50) disagree in one second. The newest copy that names storage stands, `[]` included, and a copy without the key says nothing, so `older, newer, silent` always gives B whichever is heard first. `lenient` is `requestPersistentRoomAdmission`: between copies of one second the first heard stands. `strict` is `requestPersistentRoomAdmissionEvidence`: the disagreement holds with reason `conflicting-storage`, and `contributors.storage` names the copy that stood. `orders` keys are the copies in the order heard. `randomHex` on each copy: the body nonce, the aux-rand.

storage.name: storage-relays-independent
storage.note: The relays and the nodes merge independently: the newest copy naming relays (`ind-b`, NOW + 10) is not the newest copy naming nodes (`ind-c`, NOW + 5), and each list comes from its own copy. `contributors.relays` names `ind-b` and `contributors.storage` names `ind-c`. `randomHex` on each copy: the body nonce, the aux-rand.

storage.name: storage-strict-old-reader
storage.note: Why a keeper that creates a room publishes a plain copy first: a 0.13.0 strict evidence reader refuses a body key it does not know and never retains that copy. Given a plain copy (NOW) and a copy with storage (NOW + 1), `oldStrictReader` is what 0.13.0 makes of them: `admitted`, with no storage, and `contributors` naming only the plain copy. `expected.strict` is the 0.14.0 outcome: the nodes from the later copy, `storageAt` NOW + 1. Heard with only the copy with storage, 0.13.0 strict holds with reason `unavailable` (`oldStrictReaderAlone`), so the plain copy is the only thing it can admit from. The lenient readers of both versions admit either way. `randomHex` on each copy: the body nonce, the aux-rand.
